# Standards this system follows

<!-- generated by engine.py design-md from opendesigner/state.json; change a standard with engine.py standard ..., not here -->

**Follow these rules when you build.** They come from sources marked non-negotiable, their values are locked, and `engine.py review` checks the ones it can.

This system follows OpenDesigner's house standards v4: 312 house rules.

**When to animate**
- **Decide whether to animate first.** Before choosing any tool, easing or duration, decide whether the element should animate at all (how often it is seen) and name its purpose; if either check fails, ship no animation. Values: decision-order `frequency, then purpose; only then tool, properties, easing and duration`. (STD-when-to-animate-01)
  - Why: Steps 1 (should this animate at all) and 2 (what is the purpose) gate everything: don't reach for a curve before you know whether it animates. Done wrong, animation makes an interface feel unpredictable, slow and annoying and can cost user trust.
  - Sources: ek-you-dont-need-animations, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill.
- **Name a valid purpose for every animation.** Name each animation's purpose as feedback, spatial consistency, state indication, preventing a jarring change, explanation or delight (delight only at the rare/first-time tier); if none fits, including 'it looks cool', do not animate. Values: valid-purposes `feedback, spatial consistency, state indication, preventing a jarring change, explanation, delight (rare/first-time only)`. (STD-when-to-animate-03)
  - Why: Every animation must answer 'why does this animate?'. Motion should serve a function (orient, give feedback, show relationships), not just decorate, and 'it looks cool' on a frequently seen element is a reason to stop.
  - Sources: ek-you-dont-need-animations, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-animation-vocabulary-skill.
- **Scale motion down as frequency rises.** Estimate how often a person will see each animation (100+ times a day, tens of times a day, occasionally, or rarely / first time) and make it shorter and subtler the more often it is seen, down to no animation. Values: tiers `100+ times/day; tens of times/day; occasional; rare / first-time`. (STD-when-to-animate-04)
  - Why: How often users will see an animation is a key factor in deciding whether to animate: the more often it is seen, the shorter and subtler it should be, because repeated animation stops being a pleasant surprise, becomes irritating and slows people down.
  - Sources: ek-you-dont-need-animations, eks-skills-animation-vocabulary-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-skill, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill.
- **No motion on 100+ times-a-day actions.** Give no animation to anything people trigger or see 100+ times a day, such as a launcher or command palette opening and closing, keyboard shortcuts and core navigation (on iOS and Android also tab switches, keyboard open/close, scrolling and settings toggles: platform default or nothing). Values: frequency `100+ times/day`. (STD-when-to-animate-05)
  - Sets: `motion.duration.instant` 0ms.
  - Why: Raycast is opened hundreds of times a day and has no open or close animation, which is the optimal experience; animating it every time would be very annoying.
  - Sources: ek-you-dont-need-animations, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-prototype-skill, eks-skills-prototype-picker.
- **Never animate keyboard-initiated actions.** Never animate an action started from the keyboard, including shortcuts, command-palette toggles, focus jumps and moving a list highlight with the arrow keys; the change happens instantly. (STD-when-to-animate-06)
  - Why: Keyboard actions may be repeated hundreds of times a day, and animation makes them feel slow, delayed and disconnected from the user's actions; an animated highlight lags behind the keys pressed. This is a disqualifier, not a judgment call.
  - Sources: ek-you-dont-need-animations, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards.
- **Remove or shrink motion seen tens-of-times daily.** For things people see tens of times a day (hover effects, list navigation, frequent toggles, press feedback, row selection), remove the animation, or the hover interaction itself, or reduce it to near-imperceptible, fast and subtle motion; in React Native keep it under 150ms. List navigation with the arrow keys is keyboard-initiated and gets no animation. Values: frequency `tens of times/day`; react-native-ceiling `under 150ms`; native-press-ceiling `120ms and a 3% scale`. (STD-when-to-animate-07)
  - Why: Seen tens, maybe even hundreds of times a day, animations and hover interactions stop delighting, quickly become annoying and make the interface feel slower; a hover effect used multiple times a day likely benefits most from no animation at all.
  - Sources: ek-7-practical-animation-tips, ek-you-dont-need-animations, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes.
- **Standard motion for occasional surfaces.** Give surfaces people meet occasionally (modals, drawers, sheets, toasts, settings; onboarding steps in the Expo table) standard animation, not delight motion. Values: frequency `occasional`. (STD-when-to-animate-08, should)
  - Why: The frequency tables give occasional UI standard animation and keep the delight budget for the rare/first-time tier. The Expo table lists onboarding steps as occasional, while the web tables put onboarding in the rare tier.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards.
- **Spend delight only on rare moments.** Spend delight motion (motion whose purpose is delight, such as a decorative bounce, a generous stagger or a longer beat) only on rare or first-time, high-emotion moments such as onboarding and first run, empty states, success or completion, feedback forms and celebration, and never on components people use multiple times a day. Values: frequency `rare / first-time`. (STD-when-to-animate-09)
  - Why: Seen rarely, delight is a pleasant surprise that makes the experience memorable; used multiple times a day the component quickly becomes irritating, the initial delight fades and the animation slows users down. Rare moments rendered flat are where missing delight is worth adding.
  - Sources: ek-you-dont-need-animations, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards.
- **Explanatory motion only in marketing, onboarding.** Use explanation motion (animation that demonstrates how a feature works) only on marketing and onboarding surfaces. (STD-when-to-animate-10)
  - Why: Explanation is a valid purpose only on marketing and onboarding surfaces; Linear used an animation instead of a static asset so visitors understand what Product Intelligence does straight in the initial viewport.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, ek-you-dont-need-animations.
- **Keep decoration off functional data.** Do not move data people are reading or acting on for style: keep decorative motion such as mouse-tracking, spring-driven interactive graphs and animated line drawing off functional, information-dense UI and charts, and use it only on marketing pages and illustrations. (STD-when-to-animate-11)
  - Why: Decoration on functional, information-dense UI hinders; on a functional graph in a banking app no animation is better, and a useSpring interactive graph is meant for illustrations, not functional graphs like stock charts.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, adev-changelog, eks-skills-review-animations-standards.
- **No entrance stagger on all-day lists.** Do not give a stagger or entrance animation to a list people scroll past or use all day: it should already be there. Keep staggered entrances for lists and grids seen occasionally and for content the person asked for and is waiting on. (STD-when-to-animate-13)
  - Why: The stagger recipe is for a list or grid the user sees occasionally, not one they scroll past all day; entrance animations are for content the user asked for and is waiting on.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill.
- **Say no when the gate fails.** When a requested animation fails the gate, say so plainly, write no animation code, and offer a non-motion alternative such as an instant state change or a static affordance. (STD-when-to-animate-15)
  - Why: Animating something that shouldn't animate is the worse failure mode; the gate exists to produce zero lines of code sometimes, and sometimes the best animation is no animation.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, ek-you-dont-need-animations.
- **Default to restraint when suggesting motion.** When looking for places to add motion, expect to reject most candidates: suggest at most 5-7 for a whole app and fewer for one view, list 2-4 missed opportunities separately in an audit, and say plainly when nothing survives. Values: max-suggestions-whole-app `5-7`; missed-opportunities-per-audit `2-4`. (STD-when-to-animate-16)
  - Why: An opportunity finder that suggests motion everywhere produces sluggish, over-animated interfaces; a short list of high-conviction opportunities beats a long wishlist, and if nothing survives the gate that is a good result.
  - Sources: eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-readme.
- **Delete high-frequency motion first.** Treat animation on a keyboard-initiated or high-frequency action as a blocking, HIGH-severity finding, and fix it (and any animation with no purpose) by deleting the animation before trying any tuning. (STD-when-to-animate-17)
  - Why: The remedial hierarchy starts with deleting the animation (high-frequency, no purpose, keyboard-triggered); such motion is feel-breaking, and when unsure whether motion feels right the strongest move is often to delete it.
  - Sources: eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit.
- **Goal-driven tools need no friction, not delight.** For tools people open with a clear goal (launchers, command menus, everyday work tools), remove unnecessary friction instead of adding delight motion. (STD-when-to-animate-20, should)
  - Why: A person opening such a tool has a clear goal, does not expect or need to be delighted, and just wants to work with no unnecessary friction.
  - Sources: ek-you-dont-need-animations.
- **Judge an idea before building it.** Decide deliberately whether an idea deserves to be built before building it, even when AI makes building cheap; building options A and B to compare them is good validation, but only if you actually validate the idea instead of shipping both because it costs little. (STD-when-to-animate-22, should)
  - Why: Friction used to force a decision about what was worth making; without it, vibe-coded apps and UI libraries rarely have a thought behind them and feel meaningless. Building A and B is often better validation than theorizing, but only if you actually validate the idea.
  - Sources: ek-friction-as-a-feature.

**Easing and duration**
- **Pick easing by the motion's job.** Choose each animation's easing by asking in order whether it enters or exits the screen (ease-out), moves or morphs on screen (ease-in-out), is a hover or color change (ease), or is constant motion such as a spinner, marquee or progress fill (linear), and use ease-out when none applies. Never put linear on an entrance, and put bare ease on one only when the component's personality calls for it, as the toast recipe does (STD-easing-duration-13). Values: entering-or-exiting `ease-out`; moving-or-morphing-on-screen `ease-in-out`; hover-or-color-change `ease`; constant-motion `linear`; default `ease-out`. (STD-easing-duration-01)
  - Sets: `motion.easing.linear` [0, 0, 1, 1], `motion.easing.hover` [0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1].
  - Why: Easing is the most important part of any animation; the decision order is strict so the agent does not guess or make up its own rules, and linear is kept for constant motion because progress shouldn't ease.
  - Sources: ek-agents-with-taste, ek-building-an-animation-course, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-animation-vocabulary-skill, ek-7-practical-animation-tips, adev-changelog, eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-readme, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-prototype-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes.
- **Strong custom curves, not built-in keywords.** Use the strong custom curves cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1) for ease-out and cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1) for ease-in-out instead of the built-in CSS or Reanimated easings (only the ease and linear keywords stay allowed), and take any other curve from easing.dev or easings.co rather than hand-rolling one. Values: --ease-out `cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1)`; --ease-in-out `cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1)`; EASE_OUT `Easing.bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1)`; EASE_IN_OUT `Easing.bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1)`; allowed-built-in-keywords `ease, linear`; curve-sources `https://easing.dev/, https://easings.co/`. (STD-easing-duration-02)
  - Sets: `motion.easing.enter` [0.23, 1, 0.32, 1], `motion.easing.exit` [0.23, 1, 0.32, 1], `motion.easing.standard` [0.77, 0, 0.175, 1].
  - Why: The built-in easing curves are usually not strong enough (Reanimated's are as weak as CSS's); custom curves feel more energetic and give animations the punch that makes them feel intentional.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes, ek-7-practical-animation-tips, adev-changelog.
- **Never use ease-in on UI.** Never use ease-in (CSS ease-in, Reanimated Easing.in(...)) on any UI animation, entering or exiting, and do not try to rescue it with a shorter duration; switch to ease-out. Values: forbidden `ease-in`; use-instead `cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1)`; same-duration-comparison `ease-out at 200ms feels faster than ease-in at 200ms`. (STD-easing-duration-03)
  - Why: Ease-in starts slow and speeds up at the end, delaying the exact moment the user is watching: a 300ms ease-in dropdown feels slower than the same 300ms with ease-out, and the curve itself is not made for UI animations.
  - Sources: ek-7-practical-animation-tips, eks-readme, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-prototype-skill, eks-skills-animation-vocabulary-skill, ek-agents-with-taste, ek-building-an-animation-course, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes, adev-changelog.
- **UI motion under 300ms unless justified.** Keep UI animations under 300ms. A UI duration over 300ms needs a stated reason, such as a web drawer's 500ms (STD-enter-exit-origin-41) or a toast tuned to its component's personality (STD-easing-duration-13), or it is a finding whose fix is 150-250ms. Marketing and explanatory motion can be longer, and a rarely seen, purposeful animation still has to pass this speed check: a moment that only works as a slow, showy animation gets no animation. On iOS and Android the same cap holds, but screen transitions keep the platform's default duration (iOS push 350ms) instead of being overridden. Values: ui-max `under 300ms`; fix-when-over-300ms-without-reason `150-250ms`; most-animations `0.2s to 0.3s`; faster-example `180ms dropdown`; slower-example `400ms dropdown`; native-screen-transitions `platform default (iOS push 350ms)`. (STD-easing-duration-06)
  - Why: Fast animations improve perceived performance, stay connected to the user's actions and make the interface feel as if it is truly listening: a 180ms dropdown feels more responsive than a 400ms one.
  - Sources: ek-7-practical-animation-tips, ek-you-dont-need-animations, ek-agents-with-taste, adev-changelog, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-prototype-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes.
- **Duration budget for each element.** Time each UI animation within its element's budget: button press feedback 100-160ms, tooltips and small popovers 125-200ms, dropdowns and selects 150-250ms, modals and drawers 200-500ms; on iOS and Android, press feedback 100-150ms, toggles, chips and small state changes 150-200ms, and sheets, modals and drawers a spring of about 300ms perceived. Values: button-press-feedback `100-160ms`; tooltip-small-popover `125-200ms`; dropdown-select `150-250ms`; modal-drawer `200-500ms`; native-press-feedback `100-150ms`; native-toggle-chip-small-state `150-200ms`; native-sheet-modal-drawer `spring, ~300ms perceived`; article-micro-interactions `100-150ms`; article-standard-ui `150-250ms`; article-modals-drawers `200-300ms`; recipe-press `160ms`; recipe-tooltip `125ms`; recipe-dropdown `200ms`; recipe-modal `250ms`. (STD-easing-duration-07)
  - Sets: `motion.duration.micro` 100ms, `motion.duration.short` 150ms, `motion.duration.medium` 200ms, `motion.duration.long` 250ms.
  - Why: The skills make these tables the only source of durations (no invented or approximated values), and each budget keeps its element responsive: a 180ms dropdown feels more responsive than a 400ms one. The Agents with taste article's own table is tighter for modals and drawers (200-300ms), and the recipes pick one value inside each range.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, ek-agents-with-taste, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-mobile-native-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes.
- **Nothing over 1s unless illustrative.** Never let an animation run longer than 1s unless it is illustrative (marketing or explanatory motion). The 2s linear press phase of a hold-to-confirm (STD-easing-duration-12) is a progress fill the user holds, not an animation they wait for, so it sits outside this cap [inferred]. Values: absolute-max `1s`; exception `illustrative`; marketing-scroll-reveal `clip-path 600ms var(--ease-in-out)`; marketing-image-reveal `1s cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1)`; hold-to-confirm-press `clip-path 2s linear`. (STD-easing-duration-09)
  - Why: The course's guideline 'Keep your animations fast' caps animations at 1s with illustrative motion as the only exception; unless you are working on marketing sites your animations have to be fast, and a long duration on a marketing page can be fine rather than a finding.
  - Sources: adev-changelog, ek-you-dont-need-animations, eks-skills-improve-animations-skill, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-animate-recipes, ek-the-magic-of-clip-path.
- **Duration grows with size and distance.** Give larger elements and longer travel distances longer durations than small elements and short moves. (STD-easing-duration-10)
  - Why: Stated as duration rules in the article's guidelines: larger elements animate slower than smaller ones, and longer travel means a longer duration.
  - Sources: ek-agents-with-taste.
- **Exits run about 20% faster.** Make exits faster than entrances, typically about 20% shorter (a 300ms toast entrance leaves in 250ms), rather than at the same speed. Values: exit-vs-entrance `~20% faster`; native-toast-enter `FadeInDown.duration(300).easing(EASE_OUT)`; native-toast-exit `FadeOutDown.duration(250).easing(EASE_OUT)`; web-recipes-symmetric `dropdown 200ms, tooltip 125ms, modal 250ms, same both ways`. (STD-easing-duration-11, should)
  - Why: The arrival deserves the time and the departure doesn't: the user has finished reading. The Emil design-engineering checklist flags the same enter and exit speed, but the Agents with taste article says exits 'can be' ~20% faster and the web recipes for dropdowns, tooltips and modals use one transition both ways, so this is a should; the must-level case, press and hold interactions, is STD-easing-duration-12.
  - Sources: eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes, ek-agents-with-taste, eks-skills-animate-recipes.
- **Slow deliberate phase, snappy response.** Where the user is deciding (press-and-hold, hold-to-confirm, a destructive confirm), make the deliberate phase slow (2s linear) and the system's response snappy (release in 200ms ease-out), never symmetric. Values: deliberate-phase `clip-path 2s linear`; release `clip-path 200ms ease-out`; recipe-release `clip-path 200ms var(--ease-out)`. (STD-easing-duration-12)
  - Why: Pressing should be slow when it needs to be deliberate, but release should always be snappy: slow where the user is deciding, fast where the system is responding. Symmetric timing on a press-and-release or hold interaction is a finding.
  - Sources: eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-animate-recipes.
- **Motion fits the component's personality.** Judge the product's personality before adding or reviewing motion, and let it set how much motion there is and each component's easing and duration: a crisp, professional dashboard gets fewer, subtler, crisp and fast animations, and a playful consumer app or component can have more and bouncier ones. A component whose motion does not match the rest of the product is a finding. Values: sonner-toast `transition: transform 400ms ease`; sonner-toast-enter `transition: opacity 400ms ease, transform 400ms ease`. (STD-easing-duration-13)
  - Why: Cohesion makes motion satisfying: Sonner feels right partly because its easing and duration fit the library, slightly slower than typical UI and using ease rather than ease-out to feel elegant. The Expo recipes still hold native toasts to the 300ms cap (300ms in, 250ms out).
  - Sources: eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-animate-recipes, ek-building-a-toast-component, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit.
- **Loading spinners spin fast.** Make loading spinners spin fast. (STD-easing-duration-15, should)
  - Why: A faster-spinning spinner makes the app seem to load faster even though the load time is the same, which improves perceived performance.
  - Sources: ek-7-practical-animation-tips, ek-you-dont-need-animations, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards.
- **Decide and state every curve and duration.** Choose the easing and duration of every animation deliberately while building the component, and state which curve and duration you chose and why. (STD-easing-duration-17)
  - Why: A bad easing or duration can ruin an otherwise great animation; which easing and duration were chosen, and why, is often more important than the code itself.
  - Sources: adev-home, adev-changelog, ek-building-a-drawer-component, ek-7-practical-animation-tips, eks-readme, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill.
- **Companion values follow the drawer curve.** When a script-driven value accompanies a bezier-eased transition (such as a drawer's background or theme color), interpolate it along the same curve (for example with bezier-easing), and map it linearly to drag progress only while dragging. Values: helper `bezier-easing`. (STD-easing-duration-19, should)
  - Why: Interpolating the colors linearly gives a linear transition that does not match a drawer animated with a custom bezier curve; during a drag the value follows the drag progress.
  - Sources: ek-building-a-drawer-component.

**Enter, exit and origin**
- **Never enter from scale(0).** Never animate an element in from scale(0) or out to scale(0); start from scale(0.9–0.97) together with opacity: 0, and use scale(0.95) + opacity: 0 as the replacement. Values: forbidden-start `scale(0)`; start-scale-range `0.9–0.97`; start-scale-min `0.9`; start-scale-default `0.95`; start-opacity `0`; article-demo-start-scale `0.93`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-01)
  - Sets: `motion.scale.enter` 0.95.
  - Why: scale(0) looks like the element comes out of nowhere; nothing in the real world appears from nothing (or disappears and reappears completely), and a higher start scale is like a balloon, which keeps a visible shape even when deflated.
  - Sources: ek-7-practical-animation-tips, ek-agents-with-taste, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill.
- **No opacity-only fade entrances.** Give every entering element an initial transform (a slightly smaller scale or a small translate) alongside opacity: 0; do not ship opacity-only entrances. The sources show two exceptions: under prefers-reduced-motion keep the opacity and drop the transform, and a modal's backdrop fades with opacity alone. Values: entrance-start `opacity: 0 + transform: scale(0.95) (or a translate)`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-02)
  - Why: review-animations lists pure-fade entrances next to scale(0) as an escalation trigger to flag on sight, and the audit files them under physicality, whose premise is that nothing in the real world appears from nothing.
  - Sources: eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-animate-recipes.
- **Scale popovers from their trigger.** Set transform-origin to the trigger for popovers, dropdowns, menus, selects and tooltips so they scale out of the element that opened them, never from the default center (Base UI: transform-origin: var(--transform-origin); Radix dropdown: var(--radix-dropdown-menu-content-transform-origin)). Values: base-ui `transform-origin: var(--transform-origin)`; radix-dropdown-menu `transform-origin: var(--radix-dropdown-menu-content-transform-origin)`; forbidden `transform-origin: center on a trigger-anchored surface`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-03)
  - Why: The panel should look like it came out of the thing you clicked; CSS's default origin, center, is wrong for almost every popover, and anchoring content to its source makes the spatial relationship between button and content obvious.
  - Sources: ek-7-practical-animation-tips, ek-agents-with-taste, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-apple-design-skill.
- **Keep modals scaling from center.** Keep modals at transform-origin: center; they are exempt from trigger-origin scaling and a centered modal is not a finding. Values: modal-transform-origin `center`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-04)
  - Why: Modals are not anchored to a specific trigger; they appear centered in the viewport.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill.
- **Exit the way it entered.** Make an element leave along the same path and edge it entered from, with its swipe-to-dismiss direction matching that entrance: a toast or panel that slides in from the bottom or right dismisses to the bottom or right. The web recipes express this by giving the entrance and the exit one shared state ([data-starting-style], [data-ending-style]). (STD-enter-exit-origin-06)
  - Why: Symmetric paths create spatial consistency and are what make swipe-to-dismiss feel obvious; entering from one edge and leaving to another reads as two unrelated elements.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, ek-you-dont-need-animations, eks-skills-animate-recipes.
- **Dropdowns and popovers: scale 0.95, 200ms.** Enter and exit dropdowns, popovers, menus and selects between opacity: 0 plus a slightly smaller scale (recipe: scale(0.95)) and their resting state, transitioning opacity and transform together within 150–250ms (recipe: 200ms) on the strong ease-out curve. Values: start-and-end-opacity `0`; start-and-end-scale `0.95`; duration `200ms`; duration-range `150–250ms`; easing `cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1)`; states `[data-starting-style], [data-ending-style]`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-08)
  - Sets: `motion.duration.medium` 200ms (STD-easing-duration-07 wins), `motion.scale.enter` 0.95 (STD-enter-exit-origin-01 wins).
  - Why: The panel scales out of its trigger, not out of thin air, and a short duration keeps it responsive: a 180ms dropdown feels more responsive than a 400ms one.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, ek-7-practical-animation-tips, ek-you-dont-need-animations, ek-agents-with-taste.
- **Tooltips: scale 0.97, 125ms.** Enter and exit tooltips between opacity: 0 + transform: scale(0.97) and their resting state, scaling from the trigger (transform-origin: var(--transform-origin)), in 125ms on the ease-out curve; tooltips and small popovers stay within 125–200ms. Values: start-and-end-opacity `0`; start-and-end-scale `0.97`; duration `125ms`; duration-range `125–200ms`; easing `cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1)`; transform-origin `var(--transform-origin)`; transition `transform 125ms var(--ease-out), opacity 125ms var(--ease-out)`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-09)
  - Sets: `motion.duration.tooltip` 125ms, `motion.scale.enter-tooltip` 0.97.
  - Why: A tooltip is the same shape as a popover, only faster.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-recipes, ek-7-practical-animation-tips, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill.
- **Delay only the first tooltip.** Give the first tooltip in a group a delay before it appears, then open neighbouring tooltips instantly with no delay and no animation while one is open (Base UI: transition-duration: 0ms on [data-instant]). Values: subsequent-tooltip-transition-duration `0ms`; selector `.tooltip[data-instant]`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-10)
  - Sets: `motion.duration.instant` 0ms (STD-when-to-animate-05 wins).
  - Why: The initial delay prevents accidental activation; skipping both the delay and the animation afterwards makes the whole toolbar feel faster without defeating the purpose of the delay.
  - Sources: ek-7-practical-animation-tips, ek-you-dont-need-animations, ek-agents-with-taste, eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit.
- **Modals: centered scale 0.96, 250ms.** Enter and exit modals between opacity: 0 plus a slightly smaller scale (recipe: scale(0.96)) and their resting state, kept centered, within 200–500ms (recipe: 250ms) on the ease-out curve. Values: start-and-end-opacity `0`; start-and-end-scale `0.96`; duration `250ms`; duration-range `200–500ms`; article-duration-range `200-300ms (Agents with taste)`; easing `cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1)`; transform-origin `center`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-11)
  - Sets: `motion.duration.modal` 250ms, `motion.scale.enter-modal` 0.96.
  - Why: The modal is the one popover that stays centered, because it is not anchored to a trigger; the duration tables give modals and drawers 200–500ms, and the modal recipe uses 250ms.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, ek-agents-with-taste.
- **Fade the backdrop with the modal.** Pair a modal with a dimming backdrop and transition the backdrop's opacity alongside the modal with the same timing (opacity 250ms on the ease-out curve). Values: backdrop-transition `opacity 250ms var(--ease-out)`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-12, should)
  - Sets: `motion.duration.modal` 250ms (STD-enter-exit-origin-11 wins).
  - Why: Animating the backdrop's opacity with the modal makes them read as one surface; a modal task pairs the surface with a dimming scrim.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards.
- **Stagger group entrances 30–80ms.** When several items enter together (a list or grid seen occasionally, STD-when-to-animate-13), stagger them by 30–80ms each instead of bringing everything in at once (web recipe: each item from opacity: 0 and translateY(8px) over 300ms ease-out, delays 0, 50, 100, 150ms; React Native recipe: FadeInDown.duration(250).delay(index * 40)). Values: step-range `30–80ms`; web-recipe-step `50ms`; web-recipe-delays `0ms, 50ms, 100ms, 150ms`; item-start `opacity: 0; transform: translateY(8px)`; item-duration `300ms`; item-easing `ease-out (var(--ease-out))`; react-native-recipe `FadeInDown.duration(250).delay(index * 40)`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-13)
  - Sets: `motion.duration.stagger` 50ms.
  - Why: A cascade feels more natural than everything appearing at once; longer delays make the interface feel slow, and shorter ones read as simultaneous.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes.
- **Bridge appearing and disappearing content.** Give content that appears, vanishes or swaps (conditional renders, route content, expanding sections, toasts) a short enter and exit transition instead of letting it pop in or out, unless the frequency rules say not to animate it at all. Values: entrance `scale(0.95–0.97) + opacity: 0, ease-out`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-16, should)
  - Why: Elements appearing or disappearing without a transition feel broken; preventing a jarring change is a valid purpose for motion.
  - Sources: eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, ek-you-dont-need-animations.
- **Use @starting-style for mount entry.** Animate an element's entry on mount with CSS @starting-style where browser support allows, and fall back to a data-mounted attribute set to true in a useEffect after the first render. Values: css `@starting-style { opacity: 0; transform: ... }`; fallback `useEffect(() => { setMounted(true); }, []); <div data-mounted={mounted}>`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-17, should)
  - Why: @starting-style animates entry without JavaScript and replaces the useEffect mounted-flag pattern, which still works everywhere.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-animate-recipes, ek-building-a-toast-component.
- **Slide by percentages, not pixels.** When an element slides fully in or out by its own size (a toast, drawer or sheet), express the distance as a percentage of that size, such as translateY(100%), rather than a hardcoded pixel offset. Small nudges stay in pixels in the recipes (the stagger's translateY(8px), the collapsing header's -12). Values: example `translateY(100%)`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-21, should)
  - Why: Percentages in translate() are relative to the element's own size, so translateY(100%) moves it by its own height whatever the content; this is how Sonner positions toasts and Vaul hides a drawer.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill.
- **Accordions: short height and opacity.** Animate accordions and collapses with overflow: hidden and a short height plus opacity transition (recipe: height 200ms and opacity 200ms on the ease-out curve). Values: properties `height, opacity`; duration `200ms`; easing `cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1)`; overflow `hidden`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-23)
  - Sets: `motion.duration.medium` 200ms (STD-easing-duration-07 wins).
  - Why: An accordion that snaps open needs a transition, but it is one of the few animations that costs layout on every frame, so a long duration is expensive as well as sluggish.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill.
- **Measure heights, never animate to auto.** Measure the content height before animating a collapse or expansion, and never animate to a hardcoded height (React Native) or to auto (web): measure with onLayout in React Native, and in JavaScript or through a headless primitive that supplies it on the web; or animate a transform instead. Values: measure-react-native `onLayout`; font-scale `200%`; never-animate-to `auto (web), a hardcoded height (React Native)`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-24)
  - Why: In React Native allowFontScaling is on by default, so a height measured at the default text size is wrong at 200%; on the web the accordion recipe measures the content height rather than animating to auto.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill.
- **Reveal with clip-path inset.** Reveal or hide part of an element (images, scroll reveals, comparison sliders) by animating clip-path: inset(), from inset(0 0 100% 0) to inset(0 0 0 0) on the ease-in-out curve, not by animating width, height or an overflow-hidden wrapper. Values: hidden `clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0)`; shown `clip-path: inset(0 0 0 0)`; easing `cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1)`; scroll-reveal-duration `600ms`; image-reveal-duration `1000ms (1s)`; comparison-slider `clip-path: inset(0 50% 0 0)`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-26, should)
  - Sets: `motion.duration.reveal` 600ms.
  - Why: clip-path is hardware-accelerated, needs no extra DOM elements and causes no layout shift when the image is revealed.
  - Sources: ek-the-magic-of-clip-path, eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill.
- **Scroll reveals on marketing pages only.** Use scroll-triggered reveals only on marketing surfaces, never on functional UI a user visits daily. (STD-enter-exit-origin-27)
  - Why: The recipe limits scroll reveals to marketing surfaces; a surface visited daily falls under the frequency gate, where repeated motion makes the interface feel slow, and data the user reads or acts on should not move for style.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill.
- **Fire scroll reveals once, 100px in.** Trigger a scroll reveal when the element enters the viewport and fire it only once (IntersectionObserver, or Motion's useInView with { once: true, margin: "-100px" }, which fires once at least 100px of the element is in view). Values: useInView `{ once: true, margin: "-100px" }`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-28)
  - Why: The reveal must run where the user can see it, or they never see it animate; re-animating on every scroll-by is an interface fighting its reader.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-recipes, ek-the-magic-of-clip-path.
- **Blur a crossfade that won't settle.** When a crossfade still shows two overlapping states after you have tried other easings and durations, add filter: blur(2px) during the transition (recipe: opacity 0.7, filter and opacity over 200ms ease). Values: blur `2px`; opacity-during `0.7`; duration `200ms`; easing `ease`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-29)
  - Sets: `motion.blur.crossfade` 2px.
  - Why: Without blur the eye reads two distinct objects swapping; blur blends them into one perceived transformation.
  - Sources: ek-7-practical-animation-tips, eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit.
- **Keep animated blur under 20px.** Keep any animated or transition-time blur() under 20px. Values: max-animated-blur `under 20px`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-30)
  - Why: Heavy blur is expensive, especially in Safari, and causes performance issues.
  - Sources: eks-performance-cheatsheet, eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, ek-agents-with-taste.
- **Materialize glass surfaces, don't fade.** When a glass or blurred surface enters or exits, animate its blur radius and scale together rather than using a plain opacity fade. (STD-enter-exit-origin-31, should)
  - Why: The surface then reads as a real material arriving rather than a plain opacity fade.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill.
- **Tune opacity against height by eye.** When items enter or exit a list with a height change (including reflowing toast stacks), tune the opacity change against the height animation by eye and check it again the next day. (STD-enter-exit-origin-37, should)
  - Why: The opacity change has to work with the height change and there is no formula for that pair; imperfections show up with fresh eyes.
  - Sources: eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes.
- **Set every transform-origin on purpose.** Check the transform-origin of every scaled or rotated element, SVG elements included, and set it to where the motion should grow from instead of relying on the default; verify it in slow motion. (STD-enter-exit-origin-38, should)
  - Why: Every element transforms from an anchor point whose default is center, and slow-motion review checks whether an element scales from the wrong point.
  - Sources: eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-prototype-skill, adev-changelog.
- **Mirror easing on reversible transitions.** On a reversible transition, mirror the easing so the outbound path matches the return path (inverse cubic-bézier control points for the two directions); for UI entrances and exits the ease-out rule (STD-easing-duration-01) still applies, since the inverse of an ease-out is an ease-in [inferred]. (STD-enter-exit-origin-39, should)
  - Why: Apple: if something disappears one way, we expect it to emerge from where it came.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill.
- **Vaul: --initial-transform off the edge.** When a Vaul side drawer does not touch the screen edge, adjust its enter and exit animation with the --initial-transform CSS variable. Values: css-variable `--initial-transform`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-40, should)
  - Why: The Vaul docs name --initial-transform as the way to adjust the animation when the drawer does not touch the edge. Vaul is good-to-have only: its README says the library is unmaintained (learn/sources.json, checked 2026-09-24).
  - Sources: vaul-default.
- **Drawers: 500ms on the drawer curve.** Hide a drawer or sheet at transform: translateY(100%) and open and close it with transition: transform 500ms var(--ease-drawer), where --ease-drawer is cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1); once a drag is involved it becomes a gesture and settles with a spring instead. Values: closed `[data-closed] { transform: translateY(100%) }`; open `transform: translateY(0)`; transition `transform 500ms var(--ease-drawer)`; --ease-drawer `cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)`; article `transition: transform 0.5s cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-41, should)
  - Sets: `motion.easing.drawer` [0.32, 0.72, 0, 1], `motion.duration.drawer` 500ms.
  - Why: The curve closely matches iOS (it comes from the Ionic Framework) and 500ms is meant to mimic iOS's sheet; translateY(100%) hides the drawer by its own height whatever its content, which is how Vaul hides a drawer before animating it in.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-recipes, ek-building-a-drawer-component, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill.
- **Tab color changes: clip a duplicate.** When the active tab has a different background or text color, show the change by duplicating the tab list, styling the copy as the active state, clipping the copy with clip-path: inset() so only the active tab shows (measured from the active tab's offsetLeft and offsetWidth, rounded with inset(... round r)), and animating that clip on change; do not time individual text-color transitions across the tabs. Values: active-copy-clip `clip-path: inset(0 <right>% 0 <left>% round <radius>) from the active tab's offsetLeft / offsetWidth (article example: inset(0px 75% 0px 0% round 17px))`; transition `clip-path 250ms var(--ease-in-out)`; accessibility `the copy is aria-hidden with tabIndex={-1} buttons (STD-accessibility-motion-17); the real tabs sit on an accessible primitive such as Radix Tabs (STD-accessibility-motion-16)`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-42, should)
  - Why: The text and background change together in perfect sync because one element is revealed rather than two colors being interpolated; a text-color transition is only okay-ish and can never be timed to be seamless.
  - Sources: ek-the-magic-of-clip-path, eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill.
- **Scroll-linked reveals map progress to clip-path.** Drive a reveal that follows scroll position (such as a line that grows as the page scrolls) from a scroll-progress motion value mapped onto clip-path: useScroll({ target, offset: ["start end", "end end"] }), then useTransform(scrollYProgress, [0, 1], ["100%", "0%"]), then useMotionTemplate`inset(0 0 ${clipPathY} 0)` applied as an inline clip-path style, keeping each step a motion value rather than saving it in a plain variable. Values: offset `["start end", "end end"]`; mapping `useTransform(scrollYProgress, [0, 1], ["100%", "0%"])`; style `useMotionTemplate`inset(0 0 ${clipPathY} 0)` as an inline clip-path style`; surface `scroll-driven reveals belong on marketing surfaces (STD-enter-exit-origin-27) [inferred]`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-43, should)
  - Why: The offset starts measuring when the element's top reaches the bottom of the viewport and stops when its bottom does, so the animation is not reverted when the user scrolls past it. A motion value holds the up-to-date value without re-rendering the component and updates automatically when used as an inline style; a value saved in a plain variable would not receive updates.
  - Sources: ek-the-magic-of-clip-path.
- **Theme-switch reveals use View Transitions.** Build a theme-switch reveal, where one theme uncovers the other through an animated clip-path, with the View Transitions API instead of duplicating the whole page or element and clipping the copy. Values: technique `animate clip-path to reveal the other theme`; avoid `a duplicated page or element per theme`. (STD-enter-exit-origin-44, should)
  - Why: Duplicating the element to animate is hacky and was only fine for a quick prototype; the View Transitions API achieves the same effect without the duplicate.
  - Sources: ek-the-magic-of-clip-path.

**Springs and gestures**
- **Springs for anything a finger drives.** Animate drags, flicks, swipes and any other gesture the user can interrupt or reverse mid-motion with a spring, not with a fixed-duration transition or @keyframes; motion no finger started or can interrupt runs on timing (an easing curve plus a duration). (STD-springs-gestures-01)
  - Why: Springs start from the current value and carry velocity through an interruption, while timing curves restart; a pre-scripted, fixed-duration animation cannot respond to new input. Non-gesture UI that is triggered rapidly only needs a CSS transition (STD-springs-gestures-15).
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-skill.
- **Define springs by damping and response.** Specify each spring with two designer parameters, damping ratio (or bounce) and response (or duration), rather than mass, stiffness and damping, and never treat response as a fixed duration. Values: damping-ratio `1.0 = critically damped, no bounce, smooth settle. < 1.0 = overshoots and oscillates.`; response `how quickly the value reaches the target, in seconds`; motion-apple-style `{ type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }`; motion-traditional-physics (only for more control) `{ type: "spring", mass: 1, stiffness: 100, damping: 10 }`. (STD-springs-gestures-02, should)
  - Why: Apple deliberately replaced the physics triplet with these two designer-friendly parameters, and Emil recommends the duration-and-bounce form as easier to reason about. A spring has no fixed duration: its settle time emerges from the parameters.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-animate-skill.
- **Default springs are critically damped.** Default every UI spring to critically damped (damping ratio 1.0, no overshoot) with a response of 0.3–0.4 s, and move or reposition elements with damping 1.0 and response 0.4 s; only a spring that follows a momentum gesture (STD-springs-gestures-06) or a deliberately playful or decorative moment (STD-springs-gestures-07, STD-springs-gestures-45) may be under-damped. Values: damping-ratio `1.0`; response `0.3–0.4`; move-reposition `Move / reposition (e.g. PiP) | 1.0 | 0.4`; motion `{ type: 'spring', bounce: 0, duration: 0.4 }`; reanimated `{ duration: 400, dampingRatio: 1 }`. (STD-springs-gestures-04)
  - Sets: `motion.spring.spatial.dampingRatio` 1.0, `motion.spring.spatial.stiffness` 246.7.
  - Why: Critically damped motion is graceful and non-distracting; the source calls damping 1.0 springs everywhere by default a safe house style, and 1.0 / 0.4 is what Apple ships for move / reposition.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill.
- **Bounce only after a momentum gesture.** Never let a spring overshoot on UI that appears or moves without a gesture behind it (a menu fading in, a popover, a dialog, a plain reposition); keep bounce for motion that follows a gesture that carried momentum (a flick, a throw, a drag release) and, beyond that, only for deliberately playful interactions and rare delight moments. (STD-springs-gestures-05)
  - Why: Overshoot on a menu that just faded in feels wrong; overshoot on a card you flicked feels right. Emil's skills also reserve bounce for drag-to-dismiss and playful interactions and keep it out of most UI.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill.
- **Momentum spring for released drags.** Settle or snap back a released drag with a slightly under-damped spring (damping ratio about 0.8, bounce 0.2) started from the release velocity; a settle that must stop at a hard edge, such as a sheet dismissing off-screen, stays critically damped and clamped instead (STD-springs-gestures-10). Values: apple `damping ~0.8, response 0.3–0.4`; motion-apple-design `{ type: 'spring', bounce: 0.2, duration: 0.4 }`; motion-animate-recipe `{ type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }`; reanimated `{ duration: 400, dampingRatio: 0.8, velocity }`. (STD-springs-gestures-06, should)
  - Sets: `motion.spring.momentum` {"dampingRatio": 0.8, "stiffness": 246.7, "mass": 1}.
  - Why: Settling with a spring lets an interrupted drag keep its velocity, and a little bounce is right only because a flick preceded it. The sources give 0.4 s (Apple, Reanimated) and 0.5 s (Emil's web recipe) for this spring, and the Expo recipes spring a dismissed sheet and a swipe-to-delete row that returns home at dampingRatio 1, so 0.8 is the default, not a rule.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill.
- **Keep bounce subtle, 0.1 to 0.3.** When a spring bounces, keep bounce between 0.1 and 0.3, and keep bounce out of most UI, reserving it for drag-to-dismiss and playful interactions. Values: bounce `0.1–0.3`. (STD-springs-gestures-07)
  - Why: The sources ask for subtle bounce and say to avoid it in most UI contexts.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill.
- **Sheet and drawer spring values.** Drive a sheet or drawer's spring with damping ratio 0.8 and response 0.3 s (Reanimated: { duration: 300, dampingRatio: 0.8, velocity }), about 300ms perceived, and hand it the release velocity; the dismissal spring is the exception and stays critically damped and clamped at the screen edge (STD-springs-gestures-10). The web drag-to-dismiss recipe settles with { type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }. Values: apple `Drawer / sheet | 0.8 | 0.3`; reanimated `{ duration: 300, dampingRatio: 0.8, velocity }`; perceived-duration `~300ms`; dismissal `{ duration: 300, dampingRatio: 1, velocity: e.velocityY, overshootClamping: true }`; web-recipe `{ type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }`. (STD-springs-gestures-08)
  - Sets: `motion.spring.sheet` {"dampingRatio": 0.8, "stiffness": 438.6, "mass": 1}.
  - Why: These are the values Apple ships for drawer / sheet, and the animate-expo spring and duration tables give sheets and drawers a spring of about 300ms perceived; the Expo sheet recipe dismisses with dampingRatio 1 and overshootClamping. On the web, Emil's drawer (Vaul) opens and closes with a 500ms cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1) CSS transition instead, so this spring is not the web drawer's open and close motion.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes, eks-skills-animate-recipes.
- **Spring values for rotating elements.** Rotate elements with a spring of damping ratio 0.8 and response 0.4 s. Values: damping `0.8`; response `0.4`. (STD-springs-gestures-09, should)
  - Sets: `motion.spring.rotation` {"dampingRatio": 0.8, "stiffness": 246.7, "mass": 1}.
  - Why: These are the values Apple ships for rotation.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill.
- **Independent X and Y springs.** Animate two-dimensional motion with two independent springs, one for X and one for Y, not one spring on the 2D distance. (STD-springs-gestures-11, should)
  - Why: A single spring on a 2D distance desyncs when X and Y have different velocities.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill.
- **Every animation can be grabbed mid-flight.** Make every animation the user triggers or touches interruptible and redirectable at any moment: a user can grab a moving element mid-flight and reverse it, and a closing modal or sheet that is grabbed again follows the finger instead of finishing its close first. (STD-springs-gestures-12)
  - Why: Interruptibility is the single most important principle, because the thought and the gesture happen in parallel; for anything a finger touches it is the baseline, not polish.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, ek-train-your-judgement, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes.
- **Never block input during transitions.** Never lock out input while a transition runs, a stagger included: the items must be usable before the cascade finishes. (STD-springs-gestures-13)
  - Why: Every animation must be interruptible and redirectable at any moment.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill.
- **Start from the on-screen value.** When an animation is interrupted or a drag begins, start from the element's live on-screen (presentation) value, never from its target or logical value. Values: reanimated-onStart `context.set(translateY.get())`. (STD-springs-gestures-14)
  - Why: Starting from the logical or target value causes a visible jump; without it, grabbing a sheet mid-animation teleports it.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill.
- **Transitions, not keyframes, for rapid UI.** Animate anything that can be triggered rapidly or reversed mid-motion (stacking toasts, toggles, expand/collapse, list add and remove) with CSS transitions or springs, never @keyframes. Values: example `transition: transform 400ms ease`. (STD-springs-gestures-15)
  - Why: Transitions retarget from the current value while keyframes restart from zero; with keyframes, older toasts jump into their new position instead of moving smoothly.
  - Sources: ek-building-a-toast-component, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill.
- **Carry velocity through a reversal.** When a gesture reverses direction mid-animation, carry the current velocity through the re-target instead of cutting to a new animation (on the web, use a spring library that re-targets from the current velocity). (STD-springs-gestures-16)
  - Why: Replacing one animation with another at a reversal creates a velocity discontinuity, a 'brick wall'; iOS avoids it natively with additive animations.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill.
- **Hand the release velocity to the spring.** When a gesture ends, pass the pointer's release velocity to the spring as its initial velocity, so the motion continues at the finger's exact speed. Values: motion `absolute px/s velocity directly (velocity option)`; relative-velocity `relativeVelocity = gestureVelocity / (targetValue − currentValue)`; relative-example `element at y=50, target y=150 (100px to go), finger moving 50px/s → initial spring velocity = 50 / 100 = 0.5`; reanimated `velocity: e.velocityY`. (STD-springs-gestures-17)
  - Why: Then there is no visible seam between dragging and animating; the sources call it the detail that most separates 'fluid' from 'fine'.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill.
- **Record pointer history for velocity.** While dragging, record the positions and timestamps of the last few pointermove events, not just the current point, so the velocity is known at release. (STD-springs-gestures-18, should)
  - Why: You will need the velocity at release.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill.
- **Project the flick, then snap.** On release, project where the flick would come to rest with Apple's exponential-decay function (the current position plus project(velocity)) and decide the outcome from that projected point, never from the release point or a distance-only threshold: snap to the snap point nearest the projection, so a hard flick can skip points or close a drawer, and commit a dismiss or delete when the projection passes its threshold. Values: project `(initialVelocity / 1000) * decelerationRate / (1 - decelerationRate)`; projected-endpoint `currentPosition + project(releaseVelocity)`; decelerationRate `≈ 0.998 for normal scroll feel; 0.99 for snappier`; do-not-use `v²/(2·decel)`. (STD-springs-gestures-19)
  - Sets: `motion.gesture.deceleration-rate` 0.998.
  - Why: This is what makes a flick feel like it throws the element, like scroll deceleration: a fast short swipe commits and a slow long one does not. The physics-textbook v²/(2·decel) is not what Apple ships.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes, ek-building-a-drawer-component, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill.
- **Velocity sign decides commit or reverse.** At release, decide whether a gesture commits or reverses by the sign of its velocity, not by its position. (STD-springs-gestures-20, should)
  - Why: The source's quick reference gives velocity sign, not position, as the way to decide reverse versus commit.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill.
- **A flick is enough to dismiss.** Dismiss a swiped or dragged element when its distance passes the threshold OR its velocity (absolute distance divided by the milliseconds since the drag started) exceeds about 0.11; never require distance alone. Values: velocity `Math.abs(swipeAmount) / timeTaken`; condition `Math.abs(swipeAmount) >= SWIPE_THRESHOLD || velocity > 0.11`; velocity-threshold `0.11`. (STD-springs-gestures-21)
  - Sets: `motion.gesture.dismiss-velocity` 0.11.
  - Why: A quick, short swipe should dismiss: people should not have to drag past a fixed point. Sonner's 0.11 was found by trial and error, against the average speed since the drag started, not the instantaneous release velocity [inferred].
  - Sources: ek-building-a-toast-component, ek-building-a-drawer-component, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes.
- **Sequential snap points when all matter.** When every snap point of a drawer is equally important, disable velocity-based snapping (Vaul: snapToSequentialPoint) so a fast drag cannot skip a point. Values: vaul-prop `snapToSequentialPoint`. (STD-springs-gestures-24, should)
  - Why: The Vaul docs offer it for drawers whose snap points are all equally important. This is a good-to-have source, and learn/sources.json records that Vaul's README says the library is unmaintained, so treat this as a pattern, not a dependency recommendation.
  - Sources: vaul-snap-points.
- **Rubber-band at edges, never hard-stop.** When a drag goes past a boundary, or in a direction that does not dismiss, let the element follow with progressively rising resistance (rubberband with constant 0.55) instead of stopping it dead. Values: rubberband `(overshoot * dimension * constant) / (dimension + constant * Math.abs(overshoot))`; constant `0.55`. (STD-springs-gestures-25)
  - Sets: `motion.gesture.rubberband-constant` 0.55.
  - Why: A hard stop reads as frozen, while continuous resistance reads as responsive but with nothing more there; real things slow down before they stop.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, ek-building-a-drawer-component, ek-building-a-toast-component.
- **Track the pointer 1:1 throughout.** For a drag, slider, drawer or sheet, update the UI 1:1 with the pointer for the whole interaction, keeping the element glued to the finger at the offset where it was grabbed (never snap its center to the pointer); never animate only when the gesture completes. Values: grab-offset `grabOffset = e.clientY - el.getBoundingClientRect().top`. (STD-springs-gestures-26)
  - Why: Feedback must be continuous during the interaction, not just at the end.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill.
- **Capture the pointer during a drag.** Once a drag starts, capture the pointer (setPointerCapture on pointerdown) so the drag continues when the pointer leaves the element. Values: api `el.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId)`. (STD-springs-gestures-28)
  - Why: Otherwise the drag stops as soon as the mouse or thumb moves outside the element.
  - Sources: ek-building-a-toast-component, eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-apple-design-skill.
- **Commit to a drag axis after 10px.** Require about 10px of movement along the gesture's axis before a drag or swipe takes over, then track 1:1, and always declare that axis on a pan inside a scroll view. Values: threshold `~10px`; vertical-pan `activeOffsetY([-10, 10])`; horizontal-pan `activeOffsetX([-10, 10])`. (STD-springs-gestures-30)
  - Sets: `motion.gesture.direction-threshold` 10px.
  - Why: The threshold requires intent before committing and lets a swipe on the other axis win; a pan with no axis inside a scroll view steals vertical scrolls and the list feels broken.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes.
- **Derive linked visuals from the drag.** Drive everything that follows a drag (backdrop opacity, the background's scale and corner radius) from the same drag value or drag progress, not from separate animations. Values: example `Dragging the drawer down by 40% will change the border radius to 60% of its max value`; reanimated `interpolate(translateY.get(), [0, HEIGHT], [1, 0], Extrapolation.CLAMP)`. (STD-springs-gestures-34, should)
  - Why: Values tied to drag progress stay in sync and cost nothing extra.
  - Sources: ek-building-a-drawer-component, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes.
- **Recognize gestures continuously, in parallel.** Track every plausible gesture in parallel from the first move and cancel the losers once intent is clear; do not use recognizers that only report a final state (swipeleft-type events). (STD-springs-gestures-39, should)
  - Why: Final-state recognizers throw away the continuous tracking you need for feedback.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill.
- **Remove latency from the input path.** Audit every latency on the input path (debounces, artificial timers, transition waits, the ~300ms tap delay) and remove anything that is not essential. Values: tap-delay `~300ms`. (STD-springs-gestures-41)
  - Why: The moment lag appears, the feeling of directness falls off a cliff; anything non-essential on the input path is a regression.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill.
- **Hint in the gesture's direction.** Make intermediate frames point toward the outcome (for example growing up and out toward the finger) rather than interpolating blindly to the end state. (STD-springs-gestures-42, should)
  - Why: Humans predict a final state from a trajectory.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill.
- **Spring-smooth decorative mouse tracking.** Pass decorative mouse-tracking values through a spring (Motion's useSpring) instead of tying the visual directly to the pointer position. Values: example `useSpring(mouseX * 0.1, { stiffness: 100, damping: 10 })`. (STD-springs-gestures-45, should)
  - Why: Tying visual changes directly to mouse position feels artificial because it lacks motion; a spring adds momentum.
  - Sources: eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards.
- **Feedback fires on the causal event.** Fire motion, sound and haptic feedback on the actual causal event (the toggle flipping, the item snapping home, the detent catching), not when an animation finishes, and match its character to the physicality of the action. Values: react-native-tab-example `Haptics.selectionAsync() on the press, not when the pill lands`; from-worklet `scheduleOnRN(Haptics.selectionAsync)`. (STD-springs-gestures-59)
  - Why: It must be obvious what caused the feedback.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes.
- **Visual, sound and haptic share a frame.** Fire the visual, the sound and the haptic in the same frame; never let a CSS transition lag the audio or haptic. (STD-springs-gestures-60)
  - Why: Latency between them destroys the illusion, and a haptic that lags its animation reads as a glitch, not as feedback.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes.
- **Haptics and sound only when meaningful.** Reserve haptics and sound for meaningful moments (success, error, commit, snap), and fire at most one haptic per user action: never on scroll, never per frame, never on an entrance animation the user did not cause. Values: moments `success, error, commit, snap`. (STD-springs-gestures-61)
  - Why: Over-feedback trains users to ignore all of it; used everywhere, users turn haptics off.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill.
- **Blur or stretch very fast motion.** For very fast motion, add a subtle motion blur or stretch along the direction of travel rather than moving a hard, sharp edge. (STD-springs-gestures-63, should)
  - Why: A subtle blur or stretch encodes speed and reads better than a hard sharp streak; smoothness is about what is in the frames, not just the frame rate.
  - Sources: eks-skills-apple-design-skill.

**Performance and properties**
- **Animate only transform and opacity.** Animate movement, size and visibility with transform and opacity only; never animate width, height, margin, padding, top or left (in React Native, also flex and gap), outside the clip-path, accordion-height and childless-width exceptions in STD-performance-properties-02. Values: animate `transform, opacity`; never-animate-web `width, height, margin, padding, top, left`; never-animate-react-native `width, height, margin, padding, flex, top, left, gap`; exception `width on an absolutely positioned element with no children`; indicator-sample `translateX and width with withTiming, duration 250, EASE_IN_OUT, measured once with onLayout`. (STD-performance-properties-01)
  - Why: transform and opacity skip layout and paint and run on the GPU, while width, height, margin, padding, top and left trigger all three rendering steps (layout, paint and composite), so the animation stutters. In React Native those properties re-run Yoga on every frame for the node and its siblings.
  - Sources: eks-performance-cheatsheet, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-find-animation-opportunities-skill, eks-skills-prototype-skill, eks-skills-apple-design-skill, eks-skills-animation-vocabulary-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes.
- **Only clip-path, accordion height, childless width.** For movement, size and reveals, the only exceptions to transform and opacity are clip-path and accordion height on the web, and width on an absolutely positioned element with no children (a tab pill, a progress fill). Values: fourth-property `clip-path`; height-exception `accordions only`; width-exception `absolutely positioned element with no children`. (STD-performance-properties-02)
  - Why: clip-path does not affect layout, just like transform, and is hardware-accelerated; accordions have no transform equivalent. An absolutely positioned element with no children is out of flow with no layout dependents, so nothing else re-lays-out, and animating its width keeps the corner radius that scaleX would smear.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-skill, ek-the-magic-of-clip-path, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes, eks-skills-prototype-picker, eks-skills-review-animations-skill.
- **Never use transition: all.** Never write transition: all (or Tailwind's transition-all); name the exact properties that transition. Values: instead `transition: transform var(--ds-motion-duration-medium) var(--ds-motion-easing-enter)`. (STD-performance-properties-06)
  - Why: transition: all animates unintended properties off the GPU; the animate skill lists it among the automatic blocks in review-animations.
  - Sources: eks-performance-cheatsheet, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-skill.
- **Motion: animate the full transform string.** In Motion (Framer Motion), animate the full transform string (animate={{ transform: "translateX(100px)" }}) instead of the x, y or scale shorthand props. Values: do `animate={{ transform: "translateX(100px)" }}`; dont `animate={{ x: 100 }}`. (STD-performance-properties-09)
  - Why: The shorthands are not hardware-accelerated: they run on the main thread through requestAnimationFrame and drop frames when the browser is loading, scripting or painting, while the full transform string stays smooth.
  - Sources: eks-performance-cheatsheet, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards.
- **Keep per-frame values out of React state.** Write per-frame animation values (drag, scroll or pointer position) to ref.current.style or a Motion motion value on the web, or to a Reanimated shared value in React Native; never set React state per frame. Values: web `ref.current.style`; motion `motion values (useTransform, useMotionTemplate) passed as inline style`; react-native `shared value + useAnimatedStyle`. (STD-performance-properties-10)
  - Why: Setting state every frame re-renders the component every frame, the single biggest cause of jank in React Native apps. Motion values update inline styles without re-rendering, so keep scroll-driven values as motion values end to end: copied into a const they stop receiving updates.
  - Sources: eks-performance-cheatsheet, ek-building-a-drawer-component, ek-the-magic-of-clip-path, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill.
- **Set drag transforms on the moving element.** During drags and other per-frame updates, set transform directly on the moving element (element.style.transform = `translateY(${distance}px)`); never drive it through a CSS variable set on a parent or container. Values: do `element.style.transform = `translateY(${distance}px)``; dont `element.style.setProperty('--swipe-amount', `${distance}px`)`; lag-seen-at `~20 list items`; react `ref.current.style`. (STD-performance-properties-11)
  - Why: CSS variables are inheritable, so changing one recalculates styles for every child; the drawer's drag became laggy once it held more than about 20 list items, and setting the transform on the element fixed it.
  - Sources: ek-building-a-drawer-component, eks-skills-animate-recipes, eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-emil-design-eng-skill, eks-skills-improve-animations-audit, eks-skills-review-animations-skill, eks-skills-review-animations-standards, eks-performance-cheatsheet.
- **Add will-change once you see the glitch.** Add will-change: transform as the fix for an element you have seen shift 1px or jitter as its motion starts, rather than adding it by default. Values: fix `will-change: transform`; symptom `element shifts 1px as motion starts`. (STD-performance-properties-12, should)
  - Why: The cheatsheet gives will-change: transform as the fix for an element that shifts 1px as motion starts, 'only once you see it', and the practical tips give it for shaky or jittery animations. The apple-design skill instead hints it wherever motion is imminent, so this is a should.
  - Sources: eks-performance-cheatsheet, ek-agents-with-taste.
- **Pick the cheapest animation tool.** Pick the cheapest tool that fits and stop there: on the web a CSS transition, then CSS @starting-style, then a CSS animation, then WAAPI (element.animate()), then Motion; in React Native a Reanimated CSS transition, then a Reanimated CSS animation, then layout animations, then a shared value with a gesture. Never install Motion for a hover or a fade, and use Lottie only for illustration, never for UI state. Values: web `CSS transition (hover, press, color, state toggle) > CSS @starting-style (entry, no JS state) > CSS animation (predetermined, page busy) > WAAPI element.animate() (programmatic, no library) > Motion motion.dev (springs, layout, exit, gesture-driven values)`; react-native `Reanimated CSS transition (transitionProperty) > Reanimated CSS animation (animationName) > layout animations (entering / exiting / itemLayoutAnimation) > useSharedValue + Gesture + useAnimatedStyle (anything a finger touches or derived from scroll)`; react-native-illustration-only `lottie-react-native`; react-native-huge-scene `@shopify/react-native-skia`. (STD-performance-properties-13)
  - Why: Cheapest tool that works: don't install a motion library for a fade, and using a worklet for a two-state toggle is the mobile equivalent. Motion is for springs, layout animations, exit animations and gesture-driven values; a simple hover or fade needs only a CSS transition.
  - Sources: eks-skills-animate-skill, eks-skills-pick-ui-library-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-skill, eks-skills-animate-expo-recipes.
- **Use IntersectionObserver instead of adding Motion.** If Motion (Framer Motion) is not already in the project, detect viewport entry with the Intersection Observer API instead of adding Motion for useInView. Values: api `Intersection Observer API`. (STD-performance-properties-14, should)
  - Why: Framer Motion is quite heavy.
  - Sources: ek-the-magic-of-clip-path.
- **CSS for predetermined motion, JS for dynamic.** Run predetermined motion as CSS (transitions, @starting-style, keyframe animations) or WAAPI, and keep JavaScript animation (requestAnimationFrame-driven libraries or springs) for dynamic, interruptible or gesture-driven motion. Values: waapi-example `element.animate([{ clipPath: 'inset(0 0 100% 0)' }, { clipPath: 'inset(0 0 0 0)' }], { duration: 1000, fill: 'forwards', easing: 'cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1)' })`.
